blocks.text: We have seen that linear momentum plays an important role in the translational motion of bodies; similarly, another quantity known as angular momentum has an important role in the study of rotational motion.

blocks.title: Angular momentum
blocks.text: A particle is said to possess an angular momentum about a reference axis if it so moves that its angular position changes relative to that reference axis. The angular momentum L of a particle of mass m moving with velocity v and momentum p (Fig. 3.16) relative to the origin O is defined as L = r x p ... (3.20), where r is the position vector of the particle at that instant relative to O. Angular momentum is a vector quantity; its magnitude is L = r p sin theta = m r v sin theta, where theta is the angle between r and p. The direction of L is perpendicular to the plane formed by r and p, with its sense given by the right-hand rule of the vector product. The SI unit of angular momentum is kg m^2 s^-1 or J s.

blocks.alt: From the origin O a magenta arrow r reaches a particle of mass m. From m a blue arrow p points up and to the right at angle theta to the dashed extension of r. The line of p is extended backwards as a dashed line, and the dashed perpendicular from O to it is marked r sin theta.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.16 (the second figure with this number): angular momentum L = r x p of a particle about O (original drawing after the textbook's figure).
blocks.long_description: The book prints the number Fig. 3.16 twice, once for the rigid body in topic 3.4 and again for this figure.

blocks.text: If the particle moves in a circle of radius r with uniform angular velocity omega, the angle between r and the tangential velocity is 90 degrees; hence L = m r v sin 90 = m r v, and as v = r omega, L = m r^2 omega. Now consider a symmetric rigid body rotating about a fixed axis through its centre of mass (Fig. 3.17). Each particle of the body rotates about the same axis in a circle with angular velocity omega. The magnitude of the angular momentum of the particle of mass m_i is m_i v_i r_i about the origin O, and the direction of L_i is the same as that of omega. Since v_i = r_i omega, the angular momentum of the i-th particle is m_i r_i^2 omega; summing over all particles gives the total angular momentum of the rigid body, L = (sum of m_i r_i^2) omega = I omega, where I is the moment of inertia of the rigid body about the axis of rotation. A sphere rotating in the sense of the gold arrow has its angular velocity and angular momentum taken upward along the rotational axis, as the right-hand rule shows (For Your Information).

blocks.alt: A pink disc rotates about a vertical rod through its centre, shown by a curved arrow on the disc. A right hand grasps the rod with the thumb pointing up, and a dark arrow omega points up along the rod. On the disc a line r_i runs from the axis to a particle m_i, which has a velocity arrow v_i along the tangent.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.17: A symmetric rigid body rotating about a fixed axis through its centre of mass (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.17).

blocks.alt: (a) A blue sphere on a vertical axis with a gold curved arrow round it showing its sense of rotation, and an arrow L pointing up along the axis. (b) A right hand with the fingers curled in the same sense, shown by a gold arrow, and the thumb pointing up along the arrow L.
blocks.caption: For Your Information (PDF page 67): the rotating sphere and the right-hand rule for L and omega (original drawing after the textbook's figure in this box).

blocks.title: Example 3.5
blocks.text: The mass of the Earth is 6.00 x 10^24 kg and the distance r from the Earth to the Sun is 1.50 x 10^11 m. As seen from the direction of the North Star the Earth revolves counter-clockwise around the Sun. Determine the orbital angular momentum of the Earth about the Sun, assuming it traverses a circular orbit once a year (3.16 x 10^7 s). Solution: to find the orbital angular momentum we first need the orbital speed. Moving around a circle of radius r, the Earth travels a distance 2 pi r in one year, so its orbital speed is v_o = 2 pi r / t. Orbital angular momentum of the Earth = L_o = m v_o r = 2 pi r^2 m / t = 2 pi (1.50 x 10^11 m)^2 (6.00 x 10^24 kg) / (3.16 x 10^7 s) = 2.67 x 10^40 kg m^2 s^-1. The sign is positive because the revolution is counter-clockwise.
